newsitem.title: USA: Hard-up Solv-Ex confident oil will come.
newsitem.headline: Hard-up Solv-Ex confident oil will come.

text.p: Bad publicity from official probes into Solv-Ex 's share price has left the company short of cash as it nears start up of bitumen oil production in the next few weeks, company chairman and CEO John Rendall said.
"The issue is have I enough money to survive for the next three months. No, not at the moment," Rendall told Reuters. "But we believe that once we get oil production, more money will come."
Rendall said oil production was on track to start at the end of the first quarter, but $15 million was needed to build up to 15,000 barrels per day by year end.
Solv-Ex spent $100 million in the year ending March 31, 1997, and expected to spend at least double this amount in the coming financial year, Rendall said.
He declined to say how much cash Solv-Ex has in the bank at present.

Rendall was here to attend Metal Bulletin's Bauxite and Alumina conference where he will give an update on Solv-Ex's project to produce oil, alumina and a titanium dioxide substitute from Athabasca oil sands in Alberta.
Several hundreds of millions of dollars, initially promised to Solv-Ex, "ran away" as bad publicity mounted, Rendall said.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation is probing short selling of the company's shares whose price rocketed to a high of $38 and then plunged. Solv-Ex traded on Monday at 15-1/2, up 1-1/2 in late morning trade on volume of about 325,000 shares.
The Securities and Exchanges Commission is also probing Solv-Ex share trading, Rendall added.
The U.K.'s Serious Fraud Office is investigating the link between Solv-Ex and the Morgan Grenfell Asset Management Fund whose official, Peter Young was removed from his post.
"To my knowledge, the SFO investigation will show that Peter Young has done no self-dealing at all, and in my judgement it's questionable if he's done any wrong in any way," Rendall said.
Morgan Grenfell has a 12 percent stake in Solv-Ex after buying 2.9 million of mainly restricted shares. Rendall is confident that Morgan will handle the shares properly.
Individual investors in Solv-Ex also took out a class action lawsuit against the company, alleging it is a scam that will never produce oil, Rendall said.

"I think the short sellers are behind the class action. It's not clear from the lawsuit if they have lost significant sums of money," Rendall said. "We will produce oil and that lawsuit will then become history."

Solv-Ex itself filed a lawsuit last year alleging that Zweig Co, Quilcap, consultants Weir-Jones and others signed confidentiality agreements with Solv-Ex to obtain information about the company "which was then misused", Rendall said.
Solv-Ex lawyers are moving from the discovery to the deposition phase in the New York Federal Court after obtaining documents from those listed in the lawsuit.

"We have their internal company documents which shows there was a conspiracy to attempt to stop Solv-Ex financing, and using the media and government officials in Alberta to stop the permits," Rendall said.
"This conspiracy was orchestrated by a major short seller who is a Canadian owned company. A Canadian private investigation company is linked to this Canadian short seller," Rendall said.
He declined to name the companies but said their identities would be revealed in later court documents.
However, one company, Asensio, has refused to hand over documents, Rendall added.

Rendall reiterated that several aluminum majors were enthusiastic about Solv-Ex's technology to produce cheap alumina and aluminum metal after signing confidentiality agreements to obtain data about the process.
Rendall said Solv-Ex will need $100 million to ramp up oil production to 100,000 barrels per day for which it is already applying for permits.
((Huw Jones, New York Commodity Desk 212-859-1646))
